prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Federal GIS Data Saved and Archived

Lynda Kellam

15 Dec 2025 — 2 min read

The following post was written by Frank Donnelly, the Head of GIS and Data Services at the Brown University Library and one of our DRP rescuers!

The Data Rescue Project is pleased to announce that we have archived all of the data layers from the defunct HIFLD Open GIS repository in DataLumos. This collection provides foundational geospatial layers for the nation as a whole. While useful for any type of GIS project, it is particularly important for emergency management, regional planning, and suitability analysis. The geographic features we archived represent both infrastructure and natural features: schools, hospitals, power plants, highways, rivers, flood zones, ports, mines, seismic areas, administrative boundaries, and much more. 

HIFLD Open was a portal that gathered GIS data produced by dozens of federal agencies in one convenient location. Much of the portal’s content is still available from the individual agencies that produced the datasets, and will continue to be updated by these agencies; it will just be more challenging to find and gather. The collection in DataLumos captures a final snapshot of the repository right before it went offline in August of 2025. It will be useful for data users and mappers who need easily accessible and relatively current data for the next couple of years; after that, it will serve primarily as a historic archive.

Work began over the summer of 2025, when two volunteers joined forces to download all the layers in the repository before it was disconnected. One wrote Python scripts that downloaded as much as possible using the portal's API, while the other vetted the results, identified what was missing, and created a comprehensive inventory with metadata for the records. The initiative kicked into high gear in the fall, as twenty volunteers came together and followed a documented process for uploading the data into DataLumos. One volunteer wrote a script that automated metadata entry, which was leveraged by other volunteers to accelerate the upload process. Students working in my lab identified, downloaded, and created extracts of missing datasets, and contributed to the upload process. Ultimately, 415 GIS data layers were archived.

A search for HIFLD Open in DataLumos will yield all of the records, which can be downloaded individually. The titles of the datasets and their descriptions were carried over from the old repository. Users who wish to download the entire set can follow the instructions for connecting to the Brown University Library's Globus endpoint. Globus is a mechanism for transferring big datasets; once you have a Globus account and have installed a small software package, you can search for the collection and transfer everything from a single folder. 

Many thanks to all of the volunteers affiliated with the HIFLD Open initiative at the Data Rescue Project, with special thanks to tripleshrimp, Chiara, and sefk, and to my student workers at GeoData@SciLi.

var wpcom_remote_login_extra_auth = '';
function wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_id( element_id ) {
	var dom_node = document.getElementById( element_id );
	if ( dom_node ) { dom_node.parentNode.removeChild( dom_node ); }
}
function wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_classes( class_name ) {
	var dom_nodes = document.querySelectorAll( '.' + class_name );
	for ( var i = 0; i < dom_nodes.length; i++ ) {
		dom_nodes[ i ].parentNode.removeChild( dom_nodes[ i ] );
	}
}
function wpcom_remote_login_final_cleanup() {
	wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_classes( "wpcom_remote_login_msg" );
	wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_id( "wpcom_remote_login_key" );
	wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_id( "wpcom_remote_login_validate" );
	wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_id( "wpcom_remote_login_js" );
	wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_id( "wpcom_request_access_iframe" );
	wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_id( "wpcom_request_access_styles" );
}

// Watch for messages back from the remote login
window.addEventListener( "message", function( e ) {
	if ( e.origin === "https://r-login.wordpress.com" ) {
		var data = {};
		try {
			data = JSON.parse( e.data );
		} catch( e ) {
			wpcom_remote_login_final_cleanup();
			return;
		}

		if ( data.msg === 'LOGIN' ) {
			// Clean up the login check iframe
			wpcom_remote_login_remove_dom_node_id( "wpcom_remote_login_key" );

			var id_regex = new RegExp( /^[0-9]+$/ );
			var token_regex = new RegExp( /^.*|.*|.*$/ );
			if (
				token_regex.test( data.token )
				&& id_regex.test( data.wpcomid )
			) {
				// We have everything we need to ask for a login
				var script = document.createElement( "script" );
				script.setAttribute( "id", "wpcom_remote_login_validate" );
				script.src = '/remote-login.php?wpcom_remote_login=validate'
					+ '&wpcomid=' + data.wpcomid
					+ '&token=' + encodeURIComponent( data.token )
					+ '&host=' + window.location.protocol
					+ '//' + window.location.hostname
					+ '&postid=6856'
					+ '&is_singular=1';
				document.body.appendChild( script );
			}

			return;
		}

		// Safari ITP, not logged in, so redirect
		if ( data.msg === 'LOGIN-REDIRECT' ) {
			window.location = 'https://wordpress.com/log-in?redirect_to=' + window.location.href;
			return;
		}

		// Safari ITP, storage access failed, remove the request
		if ( data.msg === 'LOGIN-REMOVE' ) {
			var css_zap = 'html { -webkit-transition: margin-top 1s; transition: margin-top 1s; } /* 9001 */ html { margin-top: 0 !important; } * html body { margin-top: 0 !important; } @media screen and ( max-width: 782px ) { html { margin-top: 0 !important; } * html body { margin-top: 0 !important; } }';
			var style_zap = document.createElement( 'style' );
			style_zap.type = 'text/css';
			style_zap.appendChild( document.createTextNode( css_zap ) );
			document.body.appendChild( style_zap );

			var e = document.getElementById( 'wpcom_request_access_iframe' );
			e.parentNode.removeChild( e );

			document.cookie = 'wordpress_com_login_access=denied; path=/; max-age=31536000';

			return;
		}

		// Safari ITP
		if ( data.msg === 'REQUEST_ACCESS' ) {
			console.log( 'request access: safari' );

			// Check ITP iframe enable/disable knob
			if ( wpcom_remote_login_extra_auth !== 'safari_itp_iframe' ) {
				return;
			}

			// If we are in a "private window" there is no ITP.
			var private_window = false;
			try {
				var opendb = window.openDatabase( null, null, null, null );
			} catch( e ) {
				private_window = true;
			}

			if ( private_window ) {
				console.log( 'private window' );
				return;
			}

			var iframe = document.createElement( 'iframe' );
			iframe.id = 'wpcom_request_access_iframe';
			iframe.setAttribute( 'scrolling', 'no' );
			iframe.setAttribute( 'sandbox', 'allow-storage-access-by-user-activation allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-top-navigation-by-user-activation' );
			iframe.src = 'https://r-login.wordpress.com/remote-login.php?wpcom_remote_login=request_access&origin=' + encodeURIComponent( data.origin ) + '&wpcomid=' + encodeURIComponent( data.wpcomid );

			var css = 'html { -webkit-transition: margin-top 1s; transition: margin-top 1s; } /* 9001 */ html { margin-top: 46px !important; } * html body { margin-top: 46px !important; } @media screen and ( max-width: 660px ) { html { margin-top: 71px !important; } * html body { margin-top: 71px !important; } #wpcom_request_access_iframe { display: block; height: 71px !important; } } #wpcom_request_access_iframe { border: 0px; height: 46px; position: fixed; top: 0; left: 0; width: 100%; min-width: 100%; z-index: 99999; background: #23282d; } ';

			var style = document.createElement( 'style' );
			style.type = 'text/css';
			style.id = 'wpcom_request_access_styles';
			style.appendChild( document.createTextNode( css ) );
			document.body.appendChild( style );

			document.body.appendChild( iframe );
		}

		if ( data.msg === 'DONE' ) {
			wpcom_remote_login_final_cleanup();
		}
	}
}, false );

window.addEventListener( "DOMContentLoaded", function( e ) {

	document.body.appendChild( iframe );
}, false );

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) Open
Organization/publisher: Department of Homeland Security
Description: The public-facing portal for the HIFLD program, providing geospatial data and tools for planners, analysts, and others throughout the homeland security enterprise, supporting missions including law enforcement, border protection, emergency management, critical infrastructure protection, and national operations and data fusion centers.
URL: https://www.dhs.gov/gmo/hifld

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Research report: Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) Open

**Research checked:** October 8, 2026  
**Overall finding:** Your description accurately captures HIFLD’s mission and DHS sponsorship, but it needs an important status correction: **HIFLD Open was discontinued in August 2025.** The broader HIFLD program and its restricted-access service, HIFLD Secure, continue. Public archives and a nongovernmental successor now provide access to much of the former Open collection.

## 1. Verification of the supplied information

| Supplied information | Finding |
|---|---|
| **Title: Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data (HIFLD) Open** | Correct historical title. However, it describes a **catalog and dissemination service containing hundreds of datasets**, rather than one homogeneous dataset. |
| **Publisher: Department of Homeland Security** | Correct at the program and portal level. More precisely, DHS’s **Geospatial Management Office (GMO), within the Office of the Chief Information Officer**, manages HIFLD. Individual layers have their own producers, sources, and stewards. |
| **Description of users and missions** | Substantially correct. DHS still describes HIFLD as supporting planners and analysts across the homeland security enterprise, including law enforcement, border protection, emergency management, infrastructure protection, and operations and fusion centers. This is now a description of the **continuing HIFLD program**, not an operating public Open portal. |
| **URL: https://www.dhs.gov/gmo/hifld** | Valid official program information page. It should not be cataloged as a currently operating public download portal for HIFLD Open. |

DHS’s current pages confirm the mission, GMO management, and Secure access arrangements. The Federal Geographic Data Committee (FGDC) explicitly states that HIFLD Open has been decommissioned. [DHS HIFLD](https://www.dhs.gov/gmo/hifld); [DHS GMO](https://www.dhs.gov/geospatial-management-office-gmo); [FGDC HIFLD](https://www.fgdc.gov/organization/working-groups-subcommittees/hifld).

**Suggested corrected catalog description**

> HIFLD Open was the Department of Homeland Security’s public geospatial infrastructure-data catalog, managed by the Geospatial Management Office. It aggregated hundreds of national-scale infrastructure, facility, boundary, and hazard datasets for preparedness, emergency management, research, planning, and other uses. Launched in February 2016 and discontinued in August 2025, its final public collection has been preserved through Data Rescue Project/DataLumos and other access initiatives. The broader DHS HIFLD program continues through restricted-access HIFLD Secure.

---

## 2. What the collection contains—and what it does not

### Nature and scope

HIFLD Open assembled foundational geospatial information useful for understanding infrastructure and the environments in which it operates. The preservation project identifies examples including:

- Schools and hospitals;
- Power plants and other infrastructure;
- Highways and ports;
- Rivers and flood zones;
- Mines and seismic areas;
- Administrative boundaries.

Program descriptions also encompass agriculture, communications, emergency services, roads and routing, transportation, and other topics. Coverage is broadly national—**all 50 states and territories at the collection level**—but individual layers differ in geographic extent and completeness. [Data Rescue Project archive announcement](https://www.datarescueproject.org/hifld-data-saved/); [NAPSG transition presentation](https://www.napsgfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/20250925-Webinar_Navigating-the-HIFLD-Transition-.pdf).

The collection includes facility locations, linear infrastructure, and polygonal boundaries or hazard areas. There is **no single shared table, schema, observation date, or update schedule** across it.

### “Foundation-level” is an important qualification

HIFLD provides a geographic foundation for analysis. It should not automatically be treated as:

- A real-time incident or operational-status feed;
- A complete census of every facility;
- An engineering-grade asset inventory;
- A definitive assessment of vulnerability;
- A list of assets officially designated as nationally critical.

The Congressional Research Service distinguishes HIFLD’s broad infrastructure inventory from the National Critical Infrastructure Prioritization Program. Inclusion in HIFLD does **not** itself confer a regulatory or official criticality designation. Some categories become relevant only in particular emergencies or policy contexts. [CRS, *Critical Infrastructure: Emerging Trends and Policy Considerations*](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48878).

### How many datasets?

Counts must be tied to a date and definition:

- At launch in February 2016, contemporary accounts describe **274 or 275 public datasets**.
- Later descriptions use “400+” or, in some presentations, “500+.”
- The Data Rescue Project reports that it ultimately archived **415 GIS layers**.

For preservation documentation, **415 is the reported final rescue count**, not proof that the public catalog always contained exactly that number. Differences may reflect catalog changes, layer-versus-item counting, or different scopes. [2016 launch announcement](https://www.napsgfoundation.org/press-release-department-of-homeland-security-makes-infrastructure-data-more-readily-available/); [DHS FY2016 annual report](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2026-03/HSIN-2016-Annual-Report.pdf); [archive announcement](https://www.datarescueproject.org/hifld-data-saved/).

---

## 3. Publisher, producers, governance, and collection process

### Program-level responsibility

DHS GMO managed the catalog, dissemination infrastructure, acquisition priorities, and user engagement. GMO’s broader role includes geospatial policy, governance, applications, and coordination across the homeland security enterprise.

Historically, the core interagency partnership included:

- Department of Homeland Security;
- Department of Defense;
- National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency (NGA);
- U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).

The partnership also drew on state, local, tribal, territorial, private-sector, and other contributors. Historically, HIFLD operated through an FGDC subcommittee accountable to the FGDC Steering Committee. **FGDC reports that this subcommittee was retired in March 2026**, with a DHS GMO HIFLD program continuing the relevant processes. [FGDC charter](https://www.fgdc.gov/organization/working-groups-subcommittees/hifld/hifld-fgdc-sc-charter-06132014.pdf); [current FGDC page](https://www.fgdc.gov/organization/working-groups-subcommittees/hifld).

### Layer-level provenance matters

DHS sponsorship does not mean that DHS directly collected every feature. HIFLD aggregated, procured, standardized, or disseminated information originating elsewhere.

A concrete example is the archived **Hospitals** layer:

- DataLumos credits **Oak Ridge National Laboratory and DHS**.
- The description says it draws on state departments and federal sources identified in a `SOURCE` field.
- Source material included PDFs, tables, and webpages, which were cleaned, geocoded, and converted into a spatial database.
- Hospitals absent from those sources are absent from the database.
- Nursing homes and health centers are explicitly excluded.

This illustrates why a national federal catalog can still contain uneven source coverage and geocoding uncertainty. [Archived Hospitals record](https://www.datalumos.org/datalumos/project/239108/version/V1/view).

### Acquisition and quality controls

DHS’s Inspector General describes a coordinated procurement process:

1. Research existing data and document a need;
2. Prioritize requirements;
3. Coordinate outreach, capture, and operations support;
4. Acquire or develop data;
5. Apply quality and publication procedures;
6. Hand datasets to operations support for HIFLD publication.

Contractors participate in research, collection, and related work. These controls are evidence of an organized process, **not a guarantee that every record is complete, current, or correctly located**. [DHS OIG report OIG-25-34](https://www.oig.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/assets/2025-08/OIG-25-34-Aug25.pdf).

---

## 4. Legal authority and policy mandate

It is important to distinguish **authority for DHS geospatial functions** from a requirement to operate **this particular public portal**.

### Direct statutory foundation: 6 U.S.C. §343(b)

The strongest direct authority is the geospatial-information provision of **6 U.S.C. §343**. It establishes an Office of Geospatial Management within the DHS CIO organization and provides for a Geospatial Information Officer.

The statute directs a program for efficient geospatial-information use, including:

- Providing information needed for critical-infrastructure protection;
- Coordinating information requirements for emergency planning, prevention, mitigation, assessment, and response;
- Assuring interoperability and preventing unnecessary duplication;
- Implementing relevant standards;
- Coordinating with FGDC;
- Supporting geospatial-data creation and sharing agreements with state, local, and tribal governments.

The geospatial provisions were added by **Section 8201 of the Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004**, amending the Homeland Security Act framework. [Official U.S. Code text](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title6-section343&num=0&edition=prelim).

### Governance and policy authorities

The 2014 HIFLD charter cites:

- OMB Circular A-16;
- Executive Order 12906;
- E-Government Act of 2002;
- OMB Circulars A-119 and A-130;
- Presidential Policy Directives 8 and 21.

These supplied historical frameworks for coordination, standards, national preparedness, and infrastructure security. They should be described as **historical charter authorities**, rather than assumed to represent every current policy arrangement. DHS Directive 034-01 separately sets departmental geospatial responsibilities. [HIFLD charter](https://www.fgdc.gov/organization/working-groups-subcommittees/hifld/hifld-fgdc-sc-charter-06132014.pdf); [DHS Directive 034-01](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/publications/mgmt/homeland-security/mgmt-dir_034-01-geospatial-management_revision-00.pdf).

### Geospatial Data Act of 2018

The Geospatial Data Act adds responsibilities concerning strategy, sharing, standards, quality, privacy, records scheduling, and avoiding duplicative collection.

Two sources are especially relevant:

- **August 2025 OIG audit:** As of December 2024, DHS met 10 of 13 responsibilities, partially met two—records scheduling and standards—and was exempt from the remaining declassification-related responsibility. The report made no recommendations.
- **FY2025 DHS self-assessment:** DHS describes the transition of public-domain foundational infrastructure data into its secure GII environment and reports that users must obtain authorized access, a government sponsor, and a Data Use Agreement.

**Interpretive caution:** The OIG assessment predates the Open shutdown in its assessment period. It is not a finding that the shutdown complied with every public-access obligation. Conversely, these sources do not establish that ending the portal was unlawful. I found no specific statutory provision requiring DHS to maintain a portal named “HIFLD Open” indefinitely. [OIG audit](https://www.oig.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/assets/2025-08/OIG-25-34-Aug25.pdf); [FY2025 DHS report](https://www.fgdc.gov/gda/gda-ca-reports/FY25CoveredAgencyReports/FY25DHSGDAReport).

---

## 5. History and major transitions

| Period | Development |
|---|---|
| **Post-September 11 period** | Infrastructure-data coordination expanded to address gaps in shared knowledge needed for homeland defense, security, and response. |
| **2002/2004 origins** | FGDC’s overview dates the initiative to February 2002, while its formal 2014 charter says the joint working group was established in 2004. Both dates appear in official documentation; the exact institutional origin is not fully reconciled. |
| **Before 2016** | Homeland Security Infrastructure Program products, including HSIP Freedom, distributed infrastructure data through physical media such as DVDs. |
| **June 13, 2014** | FGDC approved the HIFLD subcommittee charter. |
| **2015** | NGA and DHS negotiated a transition of HSIP responsibility. HIFLD also reviewed licensing conditions to identify additional layers suitable for release. |
| **February 24, 2016** | DHS announced HIFLD Open at the Esri Federal GIS Conference, replacing the HSIP Freedom DVD model with public web access, visualization, downloads, and services. |
| **2025** | DHS announced that Open would be discontinued. An initially stated end-of-fiscal-year timetable was accelerated. |
| **August 26, 2025** | Announced discontinuation date for HIFLD Open. |
| **September 16, 2025** | Transition notice identified this as the subsequent website/portal unavailability milestone. The current DHS program page is nevertheless available, so this should not be interpreted as permanent removal of all HIFLD web information. |
| **December 2025** | Data Rescue Project reported completion of a 415-layer archive in DataLumos. |
| **March 2026** | HIFLD Next launched; FGDC also reports retirement of the historical subcommittee that month. |

Sources: [FGDC overview](https://www.fgdc.gov/organization/working-groups-subcommittees/hifld); [2014 charter](https://www.fgdc.gov/organization/working-groups-subcommittees/hifld/hifld-fgdc-sc-charter-06132014.pdf); [2015 meeting material](https://www.fgdc.gov/organization/working-groups-subcommittees/hifld/meeting-minutes-hifld-sc-20150615.pdf); [2016 announcement](https://www.napsgfoundation.org/press-release-department-of-homeland-security-makes-infrastructure-data-more-readily-available/); [2025 notice](https://www.napsgfoundation.org/hifld_open/); [HIFLD Next announcement](https://www.datarescueproject.org/hifld-next/).

### Why was Open discontinued?

Contemporaneous reporting and an August 2026 presentation hosted by FGDC describe the rationale as **no longer being a mission priority**. The materials reviewed did not provide a detailed, quantified cost-benefit analysis or a comprehensive layer-by-layer security rationale.

The defensible conclusion is that DHS changed its dissemination priorities—not that all the formerly public data suddenly became classified. [Contemporaneous account](https://atcoordinates.info/2025/08/08/hifld-open-gis-portal-shuts-down-aug-26-2025/); [FGDC-hosted 2026 presentation](https://www.fgdc.gov/ngac/meetings/August_2026_Public_Meeting/HIFLDNext_LightningTalk_Aug2026).

---

## 6. Typical users and benefits to the public

### Documented user communities

HIFLD’s intended and reported users include:

- Federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial emergency managers;
- First responders and public-safety GIS personnel;
- Infrastructure-protection analysts;
- Homeland-security, homeland-defense, and law-enforcement personnel;
- Operations centers and fusion centers;
- Planners, researchers, and nongovernmental users.

The public portal extended access beyond organizations eligible for restricted systems. Civil-society successor projects explicitly support research, advocacy, policy, and mapping. No reliable portal-wide user count or demographic breakdown was established in the reviewed sources.

### Public benefits

| Benefit | Examples of applications |
|---|---|
| **Preparedness and response** | Overlay hospitals, schools, roads, or utilities with flood, wildfire, or storm footprints. |
| **Resource allocation** | Identify facilities and communities potentially needing evacuation, supplies, or service restoration. |
| **Shared situational understanding** | Give organizations a common geographic reference instead of incompatible local inventories. |
| **Planning and resilience** | Assess facility siting, service access, infrastructure exposure, and regional dependencies. |
| **Research and accountability** | Enable independent analysis of public-service geography, hazards, and infrastructure policy. |
| **Reduced duplication** | Avoid repeatedly collecting and locating the same infrastructure information. |
| **Lower access costs** | Make national layers usable without negotiating separate access arrangements for each source. |

These are documented purposes and reasonable applications, **not quantified evidence of a particular number of lives saved or dollars saved**.

A central benefit was not just access to individual files: it was **curation, discovery, standardized delivery, and convenient cross-agency aggregation**. Losing that service can impose costs even when source data remain publicly available elsewhere.

---

## 7. Access today: authoritative updates, archives, and successors

### A. Original producing agencies: best starting point for current data

DHS published a **crosswalk** linking former Open layers to source repositories, websites, or services. A preserved copy is available with a DataLumos archive index.

Use these links when current conditions matter, but verify that the replacement has the same extent, schema, and definitions as the former HIFLD layer. [HIFLD Open GIS Data Index and Crosswalk](https://www.datalumos.org/datalumos/project/241367/version/V1/view).

### B. DataLumos: preserved final collection

The Data Rescue Project reports:

- **415 layers archived**;
- Downloads captured before the August 2025 shutdown;
- Original titles and descriptions carried forward;
- Metadata captured whenever possible;
- Missing datasets identified and additional extracts created;
- A volunteer-led upload effort completed in December 2025.

This is a valuable preservation resource, but its reported completeness should not be confused with an independent audit of every record, format, attachment, or earlier version. [Archive announcement](https://www.datarescueproject.org/hifld-data-saved/); [DataLumos search](https://www.datalumos.org/datalumos/search/studies?q=hifld%20open).

### C. Brown University Library: bulk transfer

Brown provides instructions for transferring the collection through a **Globus endpoint**. This is useful for institutions seeking a full local copy rather than individual downloads. [Bulk-access instructions](https://github.com/Brown-University-Library/geodata_usgovt_backup).

### D. HIFLD Next: public nongovernmental successor

**Public Environmental Data Partners and Fulton Ring** launched HIFLD Next using the rescued collection.

Its advertised features include:

- Searchable catalog;
- Map and table previews;
- Preserved metadata;
- Versioning;
- Legacy and newer formats, including GeoParquet and PMTiles;
- A developing stewardship coalition, the HIFLD Next Commons.

It is **not DHS’s official replacement**, and a functioning successor platform does not mean every dataset is receiving current authoritative updates. Check the provenance and revision history of each layer. [HIFLD Next](https://hifld.publicenvirodata.org/); [project description](https://hifld.publicenvirodata.org/about).

### E. Homeland Security Digital Library

HSDL describes preserving an aggregation of open sources following the shutdown. It is managed by the Naval Postgraduate School’s Center for Homeland Defense and Security and funded by DHS.

Its description alone does not establish that it holds the same complete file collection as DataLumos; treat it as an additional discovery resource. [HSDL HIFLD page](https://www.hsdl.org/hifld/).

### F. HIFLD Secure

The continuing DHS service is hosted on the **Geospatial Information Infrastructure (GII)**. DHS describes it as containing commercially licensed and “For Official Use Only” data. Access requires an authorized account, profile, and approved Data Use Agreement; other transition materials identify sponsorship requirements.

Some former public layers moved to Secure. **Access restriction is not, by itself, a copyright license or classification determination.** Secure is not an unrestricted substitute for Open, and a general-purpose researcher should not assume eligibility. [DHS access instructions](https://www.dhs.gov/gmo/hifld).

---

## 8. Formats, metadata, licensing, and citation

### Technical delivery

Historically, Open used Esri ArcGIS Online/Open Data and later GeoPlatform-associated ArcGIS Hub infrastructure. It offered visualization, downloadable files, and dynamic services.

Documented historical formats include **CSV, KML, and Shapefile**. The archive inventory also identifies **file geodatabase, GeoJSON, GeoPackage, and Shapefile** holdings. Formats vary by layer; these should not be treated as universally available.

Former portal addresses include:

- `https://hifld-dhs-gii.opendata.arcgis.com/`
- `https://hifld-geoplatform.hub.arcgis.com/pages/hifld-open`

These remain useful historical identifiers even when no longer usable download locations.

### Metadata and dates

Record at least four distinct dates:

1. Underlying observation or source date;
2. Dataset revision date;
3. Archive capture date;
4. Repository deposit/publication date.

For example, the archived Hospitals record lists a **June 30, 2024 time period**, but a **2025 DataLumos publication date**. Calling it “2025 hospital data” solely because it was deposited in 2025 would be misleading.

The archive index includes titles, filenames, dates, descriptions, terms, formats, sizes, standardized publishers, and repository links. Metadata was preserved **where available**, not necessarily uniformly.

### Rights and licensing

HIFLD Open was characterized as providing public-domain data. Nevertheless:

- Inspect each layer’s original use constraints and source terms.
- Do not infer that every contributing organization’s work is a U.S. federal-government work.
- Do not assign a blanket CC0 license without layer-level evidence.
- Keep dataset rights separate from repository terms and successor-platform software licenses.
- Do not assume a Secure Data Use Agreement permits public redistribution.

For example, HIFLD Next’s implementation is described as open source under **AGPL-3.0**; that software license is not a blanket license for every dataset it serves. [Fulton Ring technical description](https://fultonring.com/work/hifld-next/).

### Citation

Prefer **layer-level, version-specific citations** over a generic citation to HIFLD.

An available example is:

> Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and United States Department of Homeland Security. *HIFLD OPEN Hospitals*. Inter-university Consortium for Political and Social Research [distributor], 2025-10-22. https://doi.org/10.3886/E239108V1

For analysis, also record the source-data date, download date, format, and any transformations performed.

---

## 9. Data-science limitations and validation requirements

The following are practical checks, not claims that every HIFLD layer has each defect:

- **Completeness:** Compare against sector-specific inventories. Missing features may reflect missing sources, not nonexistent facilities.
- **Temporal accuracy:** Confirm openings, closures, relocations, ownership changes, and capacity updates.
- **Positional accuracy:** Distinguish address-geocoded points from surveyed locations or actual footprints.
- **Duplicates:** Check whether campuses, subsidiaries, or co-located facilities appear as separate records.
- **Missing values:** Separate unknown, unavailable, and zero values.
- **Schema changes:** Replacement feeds may rename fields, change categories, or use different identifiers.
- **Spatial reference:** Read the actual coordinate-system metadata; do not assume one projection across the catalog.
- **Format fidelity:** Shapefile exports can truncate field names or lose richer schema information.
- **API completeness:** When using surviving ArcGIS services, handle pagination and compare retrieved counts with service counts.
- **Longitudinal comparability:** A difference between snapshots may reflect a corrected geocode or definition change rather than real-world infrastructure change.

The Hospitals documentation gives a particularly clear warning: **facilities absent from its source lists are absent from the dataset**. A national scope does not establish census completeness.

For emergency operations, validate consequential findings against current authoritative sources and local knowledge. A rescued snapshot is not a live operational feed.

---

## 10. Preservation priorities

### Preserve the catalog context, not only the geometries

A strong preservation package should contain:

1. Original downloaded files;
2. Original metadata, including XML where present;
3. Catalog inventory and JSON records where available;
4. DHS crosswalk;
5. Field definitions, coded-value domains, and use constraints;
6. Original item IDs, service URLs, and layer numbers where recoverable;
7. Capture logs, dates, checksums, feature counts, and extents;
8. Shutdown notices, charters, and program documentation;
9. A provenance distinction between original downloads, reconstructed extracts, and converted formats;
10. Links to current sources and successor versions.

### Preserve originals and normalized copies separately

Retain original packages unchanged. Create open-format derivatives for accessibility, but document conversions and validate counts, geometry, attributes, encoding, and coordinate systems.

Use redundant institutional storage and periodic fixity checks. A mirror without metadata or a conversion without provenance may preserve usable features while losing their evidentiary value.

### Key unresolved preservation questions

The reviewed materials do not establish:

- Complete preservation of all earlier annual versions;
- Complete coverage of every historical attachment or ancillary file;
- A comprehensive public export of Secure holdings;
- HIFLD Open’s specific NARA disposition authority;
- A guaranteed update schedule for the rescued collection.

The OIG’s finding that DHS **only partially met the records-scheduling responsibility** makes retention and disposition documentation an especially useful follow-up topic.

---

## 11. Policy and accountability questions

The shutdown raises questions beyond whether copies survived.

### Public-access equity

Restricted access introduces sponsorship, approval, and agreement requirements. These may affect journalists, researchers, community organizations, and smaller jurisdictions differently.

### Cost shifting

Decentralizing discovery can transfer work from a federal curator to users who must locate, reconcile, validate, and monitor many separate sources.

### Reproducibility

Current feeds are useful operationally; dated snapshots are necessary to reproduce historical analyses. Neither replaces the other.

### Stewardship and authority

Volunteer rescue and nonprofit delivery restore access, but they do not automatically replace federal collection capacity, agency relationships, funding, or authoritative maintenance.

### Useful oversight or records requests

A preservationist or activist could seek:

- The shutdown decision memorandum and alternatives analysis;
- Operating costs, contracts, staffing, and documented savings;
- A complete inventory of layers migrated, redirected, or discontinued;
- Layer-specific maintenance commitments;
- Sponsorship and access-approval criteria;
- Records schedules and disposition instructions;
- Any layer-specific security or licensing analyses;
- Transition impact assessments and user feedback.

The reviewed sources did **not** establish a separate HIFLD Open budget, quantified shutdown savings, or a measured public-impact assessment.

---

## 12. Research confidence and limitations

**High-confidence findings:** DHS GMO management; the collection’s multi-dataset nature; February 2016 launch; August 2025 discontinuation; continuing Secure service; the rescue project’s reported 415-layer archive; and HIFLD Next’s existence.

**Unresolved or qualified findings:** Exact early founding date; reconciliation of changing layer counts; independently audited archive completeness; detailed shutdown economics; and comprehensive layer-by-layer maintenance status.

This report draws on official DHS, FGDC, U.S. Code, OIG, and CRS materials, supplemented by contemporary public-safety announcements, archival repository descriptions, and preservation-project documentation. Some repository pages blocked direct retrieval, and PDF access was limited; their indexed text supplied relevant evidence. **I did not download and audit all 415 layers**, so collection-wide technical guarantees would be inappropriate.

## Bottom line

**HIFLD Open was a federally managed public geospatial catalog whose value lay in both its data and its cross-agency curation.** DHS’s underlying geospatial responsibilities continue, but unrestricted access through the original portal does not.

For current analysis, start with the **preserved DHS crosswalk and original producers**. For historical evidence and preservation, use **DataLumos and Brown’s bulk archive**. For convenient public discovery and newer delivery formats, use **HIFLD Next**, while clearly distinguishing rescued federal snapshots from subsequently updated nongovernmental versions.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.

# HIFLD Open: dataset risk assessment

**Assessment date: October 8, 2026**

## Overall finding and scope

**Removal from the primary public distribution location has already occurred.** DHS discontinued HIFLD Open in August 2025. This is therefore an assessment of an actual loss of federal public access, not merely a forecast.

However, **the underlying infrastructure data have not all disappeared**:

- The Data Rescue Project reports preserving **415 layers** in DataLumos.
- Many producing agencies continue publishing their own datasets.
- Some former Open layers moved to restricted-access **HIFLD Secure**.
- **HIFLD Next**, a nongovernmental successor, provides public access and some subsequent updates.

The ratings below assess **HIFLD Open as a publicly accessible, federally curated collection**, not every contributing agency’s collection or the continuing Secure program.

Two rubric interpretations matter:

1. **Historical availability:** I consider removal from the original federal distribution service a risk even where external archives mitigate the loss. I do not equate that removal with disappearance of every public copy.
2. **“Gone” for future availability, quality, and policy:** This describes termination of the **Open publication service**. It does not mean all underlying data collection has stopped.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — not supported for public copies overall.** The Data Rescue Project reports archiving all 415 layers present immediately before shutdown. DataLumos provides individual records; Brown University Library supports bulk transfer. Thus, a substantial historical collection remains publicly accessible.  
  Sources: [archive announcement](https://www.datarescueproject.org/hifld-data-saved/); [preserved index and DHS crosswalk](https://www.datalumos.org/datalumos/project/241367/version/V1/view).

- **High Risk — supported at the original federal location.** DHS removed the Open distribution service. The transition notice states that layers hosted only there would move to Secure, while selected layers would be available through original providers. This eliminated unrestricted federal access through the original catalog and services.  
  Sources: [NAPSG transition notice](https://www.napsgfoundation.org/hifld_open/); [FGDC confirmation of decommissioning](https://www.fgdc.gov/organization/working-groups-subcommittees/hifld/index_html).

- **Moderate Risk — no demonstrated collection-wide deletion of specific historical fields.** Metadata were preserved “whenever possible,” but that is a preservation limitation, not proof that DHS selectively removed particular attributes.  
  Source: [archive index documentation](https://www.datalumos.org/datalumos/project/241367/version/V1/view).

- **No Known Issue — partially supported by the rescue.** The final pre-shutdown snapshot survives. However, the archive does not establish preservation of every earlier version, original service, attachment, or metadata record.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

The original federal public collection was removed, although external archives substantially reduce the risk of total historical loss.

**Qualification:** If your implementation measures only whether the **final snapshot remains available anywhere**, rather than availability at its primary location, **No Known Issue** is defensible for that snapshot. It is not established for the complete historical version series.

---

## 2. Future Data Availability

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — supported for HIFLD Open.** The Open publication service was discontinued on August 26, 2025; FGDC now explicitly describes it as decommissioned. DHS’s 2026 user-forum description also confirms the discontinuation.  
  Sources: [transition notice](https://www.napsgfoundation.org/hifld_open/); [FGDC](https://www.fgdc.gov/organization/working-groups-subcommittees/hifld/index_html); [2026 DHS program recap](https://www.dhs.gov/medialibrary/assets/video/68057).

- **High or Moderate Risk — delay-based criteria are not the best fit.** This was a termination, not a missed publication date. I found no HIFLD Open-specific statutory publication deadline or collection-wide ICR whose expiration explains the shutdown.

- **No Known Issue — applies only to parts of the wider ecosystem.** Producing agencies continue updating many layers, and the broader HIFLD program remains active. DHS’s 2026 “State of the Data” presentation describes updates and additions from agencies, vendors, and Oak Ridge National Laboratory.  
  Sources: [archive announcement](https://www.datarescueproject.org/hifld-data-saved/); [DHS 2026 data presentation description](https://www.dhs.gov/medialibrary/assets/video/68058).

### Selected level: **Gone**

There is no continuing federal **HIFLD Open publication cycle**. Continued source-agency or Secure updates do not restore that unrestricted, centrally curated service.

---

## 3. Data Quality

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — supported under the rubric’s termination criterion.** HIFLD Open no longer publishes or maintains its public collection.

- **High Risk — supported for present-day use of the rescued snapshot.** The archive captures conditions before the August 2025 shutdown. Without subsequent updates, facility openings, closures, relocations, and attribute changes will progressively reduce its timeliness. The archivists explicitly describe its eventual role as primarily historical.  
  Source: [archive announcement](https://www.datarescueproject.org/hifld-data-saved/).

- **Moderate Risk — supported for fragmented replacement workflows.** Users must reconcile different source services, schemas, identifiers, and update schedules. NAPSG’s transition presentation warns that former Open layers become more brittle without DHS centralization.  
  Source: [September 2025 transition presentation](https://www.napsgfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/20250925-Webinar_Navigating-the-HIFLD-Transition-.pdf).

- **No Known Issue — supported for some individual replacements, not the entire collection.** HIFLD Next offers version tracking, modern formats, and quality-feedback mechanisms. An August 2026 presentation identifies an updated hospitals layer. These improvements do not establish current maintenance of every former Open layer.  
  Source: [FGDC-hosted HIFLD Next presentation](https://www.fgdc.gov/ngac/meetings/August_2026_Public_Meeting/HIFLDNext_LightningTalk_Aug2026).

### Selected level: **Gone**

This follows the rubric for the terminated Open service. **For surviving copies themselves, the principal problem is timeliness—not evidence that the historical files were falsified or corrupted.** An accurate historical snapshot can still be unsuitable for current emergency operations.

---

## 4. Statutory Context

### Evidence by risk level

- **High Risk — supported for the specific public portal.** No reviewed statute expressly requires a service named HIFLD Open, its exact layer inventory, or indefinite unrestricted publication through that portal. Alternative producing-agency collections exist for many layers.

- **Moderate Risk — only partly supported.** HIFLD supports federal implementation, but the rubric’s “no alternatives” condition is not satisfied collection-wide.

- **No Known Issue — substantial counterevidence.** **6 U.S.C. §343(b)** expressly establishes the Geospatial Management Office and requires a program supporting critical-infrastructure protection, emergency functions, interoperability, and coordination. HIFLD also has documented programmatic users.  
  Sources: [statutory text](https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title6-section343&num=0&edition=prelim); [CRS infrastructure report](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R48878).

A particularly concrete federal use appears in the **Federal Transit Administration’s Capital Investment Grants program**. Its October 1, 2026 proposed guidance would remove an “access to essential services” subfactor because the HIFLD data used for that measure are unavailable. This proposal remains pending, with comments due November 16, 2026.  
Source: [Federal Register, October 1, 2026](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/01/2026-20179/notice-of-availability-of-proposed-policy-guidance-for-the-capital-investment-grants-program).

### Selected level: **High Risk**

The broader geospatial mission has clear statutory backing, **but the Open dissemination mechanism lacks equally specific protection**, and alternatives can substitute for parts of the collection. Its demonstrated federal use did not prevent discontinuation.

This is a portal-specific rating, not a claim that GMO lacks statutory authorization or that HIFLD has no programmatic use.

---

## 5. Staffing and Funding

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — not supported.** GMO and HIFLD remain operational; DHS held a 2026 user forum. There is no evidence that all relevant staff or funding were eliminated.

- **High Risk — supported by the rubric’s absolute agency-level staffing threshold.** GAO reports DHS’s civilian workforce falling from **231,337 in December 2024 to 229,342 in January 2026**: a net reduction of **1,995 employees**, or approximately **0.9%**. This exceeds the rubric’s alternative threshold of **1,000 staff lost**, despite the small percentage reduction.  
  Source: [GAO-26-108583, Table 1](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-26-108583.pdf).

- **Moderate Risk — additional organizational concerns, but insufficient unit-level measurements.** April 2025 reporting described plans to cut the Management Directorate by roughly 50%. That was a reported target, **not proof of an achieved 50% reduction**. OCIO was subsequently reorganized, and its leadership changed in August 2026.  
  Sources: [workforce-cut plans](https://federalnewsnetwork.com/management/2025/04/dhs-plans-to-slash-hq-workforce-including-ai-experts/); [CIO transition](https://federalnewsnetwork.com/cio-news/2026/08/dhs-expected-to-tap-doge-staffer-as-next-cio/).

- **No Known Issue — meaningful budget and staffing counterevidence.**
  - DHS OIG reports GMO increased from seven to **10 federal employees** between October 2022 and September 2024.
  - The FY2026 budget **request** proposed OCIO funding increasing from **$627.854 million to $642.424 million**, approximately **2.3%**, with FTE increasing from 519 to 543.
  - These are older staffing observations and proposed parent-office resources—not verified current HIFLD Open allocations.  
  Sources: [DHS OIG](https://www.oig.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/assets/2025-08/OIG-25-34-Aug25.pdf); [FY2026 budget justification](https://www.dhs.gov/sites/default/files/2025-06/25_0613_mgmt_fy26-congressional-budget-justificatin.pdf).

### Staffing-tracker check

The requested [USAJobs tracker](https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com) says it tracks **job advertisements, not employees or completed hires**, and announces that collection stopped December 31, 2025. It cannot establish a current GMO headcount or a percentage of staff lost. I therefore used GAO workforce figures rather than converting advertisement changes into staffing losses.

### Selected level: **High Risk**

This is a **literal application of the agency-level 1,000-person threshold**. Confidence is high in the DHS-wide figures but low in their explanatory value for HIFLD: **no verified post-2024 GMO headcount or HIFLD-specific funding reduction was found**.

---

## 6. Policy

### Evidence by risk level

- **Gone — directly supported.** DHS implemented termination of public Open publication in 2025.

- **High Risk — also supported, but superseded by termination.** The policy shift replaced centralized unrestricted dissemination with source-provider access and, for some layers, Secure access requiring authorization and a Data Use Agreement. A presentation hosted by FGDC describes the rationale as “no longer a national mission priority”; that attribution is not itself a DHS decision memorandum.  
  Sources: [transition notice](https://www.napsgfoundation.org/hifld_open/); [current DHS access requirements](https://www.dhs.gov/gmo/hifld); [FGDC-hosted presentation](https://www.fgdc.gov/ngac/meetings/August_2026_Public_Meeting/HIFLDNext_LightningTalk_Aug2026).

- **Moderate Risk — supported for downstream pending changes.** FTA now proposes removing a grant-evaluation subfactor because of the loss of HIFLD availability. Its November 2025 final guidance had already acknowledged problems caused by unavailable HIFLD urgent-care data.  
  Sources: [2026 proposed guidance](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/01/2026-20179/notice-of-availability-of-proposed-policy-guidance-for-the-capital-investment-grants-program); [2025 final guidance](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/11/12/2025-19848/notice-of-availability-of-final-policy-guidance-for-the-capital-investment-grants-program).

- **No Known Issue — not supported.** A consequential publication-policy change occurred after January 2025.

### Selected level: **Gone**

The relevant public-publication policy change is implemented. **I found no basis to attribute the shutdown specifically to a presidentially directed ICR, nor evidence that all former Open data became classified.**

---

## Practical conclusion

**The principal remaining risk is loss of dependable, current public updates—not immediate disappearance of the rescued historical snapshot.** Preservation has materially mitigated historical loss, but it has not automatically replaced federal maintenance, consistent metadata, stable services, or authoritative update schedules.

For users:

- Preserve the DataLumos files, metadata, index, and DHS crosswalk locally.
- Use original producers for current data and verify equivalence to former HIFLD layers.
- Treat HIFLD Next as a useful successor, checking provenance and update dates layer by layer.
- Do not treat restricted Secure access as a universal public replacement.
- Distinguish **archive capture date** from **underlying data currency**.

## Summary of risk levels

Historical Data Availability: **High Risk**  
Future Data Availability: **Gone**  
Data Quality: **Gone**  
Statutory Context: **High Risk**  
Staffing and Funding: **High Risk**  
Policy: **Gone**
